articles.title: Deejay Boboss becomes Nairobi street sensation with wooden DJ deck
articles.description: Kenya is home to a vibrant community of skilled electronic repairers who breathe new life into devices long considered obsolete or beyond repair. A young deejay has assembled a homemade deck from discarded materials such as radio motherboards, plywood, plastic bottle caps, towel holders and a fork. Deejay Boboss says he has often encountered people who accuse him of playing music from his smartphone rather than using his homemade deck. But their doubts quickly turn into amazement whenever he uses a fork to produce scratch effects, leaving onlookers laughing in disbelief and urging him to repeat the trick.

articles.title: Fitting a resume to the page automatically, without breaking it for ATS parsers
articles.description: This is a layout problem, not an AI problem. Every HTML-to-PDF generator eventually runs into it: the last page that holds only a couple of lines. I'll cover how we hit it, the options we weighed, why predicting page breaks is a dead end, and the trick we ended up using, which is to let the browser measure the layout instead of guessing it. If you generate PDFs from HTML, some of this should be directly reusable. The situation I'm the founder of CV by JD. We rewrite resumes for specific job descriptions, and when you're happy with the result, you download it as a PDF. A resume PDF has two readers. One is a person, often a recruiter skimming a stack of applications. The other is an ATS (applicant tracking system), the software employers use to pull the text out of a resume and search it. A good PDF has to look finished to the first reader and stay easy to parse for the second. How we got here We render PDFs on our server with headless Chrome, a copy of the Chrome browser with no window, controlled by code (puppeteer-core with a serverless Chromium build). The PDF uses exactly the same HTML and CSS as the preview in the app, so what you see is what you download: In your browser On our server ─────────────── ───────────── Resume preview ── "Download" ─▶ The same HTML and CSS, opened in (HTML + CSS) headless Chrome and printed to PDF ◀── resume.pdf ── We offer five templates, each with its own fonts, spacing and margins. The templates were designed for a "typical" resume. Real resumes aren't typical. Some are half a page, some are four pages, and they almost never end neatly at the bottom of a page. The problem My own resume was the test case. In one template it ran to four pages, and page four held two lines from the education section followed by white space all the way down. Nothing was wrong with the content. It just looked unfinished, and that's the first impression a reader gets. The usual fix is manual: open the file in Word, use "Shrink One Page", nudge the margins, and export again. We wanted every export to fit its pages well, automatically, for every template, without ever looking cramped and without changing what an ATS reads. What we researched We started by looking at how existing tools handle this. Word's "Shrink One Page" reduces font sizes until the document loses a page. Some resume builders give you sliders for spacing, margins and font size, and leave it to you. Both approaches confirmed the same toolbox: vertical spacing, line height, margins and font size. Both also showed the risk. Shrink too far and the page looks crammed, and text at 8pt is hard to read. Thinking through how to do this automatically, three constraints narrowed the design: Free knobs can combine badly. If spacing, line height, margins and font size can each move freely, some combinations fit the page but look wrong, like tiny text inside wide margins. Word counts don't predict page breaks. Headings that won't sit alone at the bottom of a page, list items that won't split and long URLs all move where a page ends. Two resumes with the same word count can end on different pages. Rendering real PDFs to search for a setting is slow. The first PDF render after a serverless function starts up takes a few seconds. Trying many settings for every download would keep users waiting. The options we found For what to adjust: Option Problem Shrink only the font, as Word does Gets small quickly, and does nothing for a page that's too empty Search four independent knobs Finds strange combinations, and is hard to test or explain One "fit level" that moves all four together, within limits Fewer possible outcomes, but every one of them looks designed For how to decide: Estimate from word count Wrong too often, because page breaks depend on layout Render real PDFs at several settings and pick one Accurate, but takes many seconds per download Have the browser lay the document out as pages and measure it, without printing Needs a clever setup, but it's accurate and fast What we chose, and why One number per document Each document gets one fit level, a whole number from −8 to +8. Think of it as a single dial: negative values tighten the layout, positive values loosen it. Level 0 is the template exactly as designed. Each other level is a fixed mix of small changes: vertical spacing, between 70% and 130% of the original line height, within fixed bounds side margins, between 0.35 and 0.58 inches font size, never below 9.5pt for body text The four settings change together in a fixed order, so none of them runs out of room before the others. When shrinking, spacing tightens first and font size changes last. When growing, margins widen last, because wider margins frame a short page well. If a template's text is already small, we never shrink it further. We chose this because 17 levels is a small, testable set, and every level looks like a deliberate design rather than an accident. Let the browser measure the pages This is the part I'd most like other people to reuse. Printing and CSS columns split content the same way. Content flows down a box of fixed height, and when the box is full it continues in the next one. In Chrome, both use the same layout engine. So if you put the resume in a hidden container whose columns are exactly the size of one printed page's content area, Chrome breaks it into "pages" for you, side by side on screen: ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ page 1 │ │ page 2 │ │ page 3 │ │ page 4 │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██ │ ◀ 4 columns = 4 pages, │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ │ and the last one is │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ ██████ │ │ │ only about 10% full └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ The CSS is short: Count the columns and you have the page count. Measure how far the content reaches down the last column and you know how full the last page is. This happens in an ordinary layout pass, with no PDF rendering. Most documents are settled by measuring level 0 alone. When they aren't, a small script inside the page applies each of the 17 levels' styles in turn, lets Chrome lay the document out again, and reads the page count and fill each time, which still takes a fraction of the time of a single PDF render. One detail matters a lot here. Chrome rounds the printed page's content height up to a whole pixel. On US Letter paper with our margins, the content area works out to 979.2 CSS pixels tall, but Chrome prints it as 980. If you measure with 979.2, a nearly full page gets predicted as spilling onto the next one, and you pick the wrong level. Round up the same way and the predictions match. A simple rule for choosing the level With the page count and the fullness of the last page measured at level 0: What we see What we do One page Leave it alone More than four pages Leave it alone. The content needs cutting, not squeezing Last page 30% full or less Shrink just enough to remove that last page, picking the mildest level that does it. The new last page must stay under about 97% full, so it doesn't look crammed, and shrinking mustn't leave a big blank at the bottom of an earlier page because a block that can't be split, such as a job entry, got pushed onto the next page. If no level qualifies, leave it Last page between 30% and 60% full Grow slightly so the pages fill more evenly, but only if it keeps the same page count and actually helps Fuller than that The thinking behind the thresholds: below 30%, the leftover content is small enough that a modest shrink usually absorbs it. Between 30% and 60%, losing the page would need too much squeezing, so evening out the pages looks better. We tuned these thresholds by rendering 150 test resumes of different lengths at every level as real PDFs and comparing the results. For my resume, that turned four pages, the last one almost empty, into three pages with the last one nearly full. Check the real output In the user's browser, the preview runs the same measurement and picks a level, so what you see matches what you'll download. When you click Download, the server measures again in headless Chrome, prints the PDF, and then counts the pages in the actual file. If the count doesn't match the prediction, it prints again at level 0. We'd rather send the template as designed than a surprise. Protect the second reader Fitting must not change what an ATS extracts. Two rules guarantee that: A document at level 0 is byte-for-byte unchanged. At level 0 we don't add the fitting styles at all, so Chrome receives exactly the HTML it did before this feature existed. The extracted words never change. Our tests render every template at every level, extract the text with pdftotext, and check that the words match level 0 exactly. That second test caught a real bug. One template used letter-spacing in em units on its uppercase section headings. At a larger font size the spacing grew enough that pdftotext read "SUMMARY" as "S U M M A R Y", seven one-letter words. An ATS could read it the same way, and a keyword search for "summary" would miss it. We now set heading letter-spacing in pixels. What you can take from this If the browser can lay it out, the browser can measure it. Multi-column layout makes a surprisingly good page simulator, and it's far faster than rendering PDFs. One bounded setting beats several free ones. It's easier to test, easier to explain, and it can't produce strange combinations. Match the browser's rounding, or your predictions will be off on exactly the pages that matter most: the nearly full ones. Check the real output and keep a safe fallback for when the prediction is wrong. If machines read your documents, test what they extract, not just what people see. Have you used CSS layout as a measuring tool for something else? I'd like to know what else it's good for.

articles.title: Getting Started with NVIDIA Brev: Cloud GPUs, Credits, and Cost Management
articles.description: NVIDIA Brev is a cloud-GPU development platform for AI and machine-learning projects. It brings together GPU resources from cloud providers and helps deploy environments with common tools such as CUDA, Python, and Docker. This CAVEDU walkthrough covers registration, credits, billing, Launchables, and resource management. It is a guide to the interface shown in the source article, not a statement of current pricing or contractual terms. Before you begin Brev is a paid cloud service. Adding funds, deploying environments, or enabling auto-recharge can create real charges. Check the current platform terms, provider prices, taxes, credit rules, and refund conditions before paying. Confirm the account and team, the authorized payment method, the amount, and whether auto-recharge is enabled. Before deployment, inspect the Launchable and hardware configuration. After use, stop or delete unneeded resources as appropriate. Stopping compute can leave storage charges; back up important data before deleting anything. Use a Windows, macOS, or Linux computer with a modern browser, JavaScript and cookies enabled, and a stable Internet connection. 1. Register and sign in Open NVIDIA Brev and choose Sign In. Enter your email and continue. Existing NVIDIA accounts may proceed directly to cloud-account setup. For a new account, follow the password and verification steps, retrieve the email verification code, and complete the account setup. The source chooses to defer passkey setup; choose your preferred supported authentication method. Review the privacy options and terms rather than assuming the source’s choices are appropriate for every account. At first sign-in, you may be asked to name and create an NVIDIA Cloud Account. If your NVIDIA account already has one, this step may be skipped. Complete the applicable Brev terms step to reach the dashboard. 2. Payment methods and credits Open Billing or Add Credits. Connect a card opens payment-method entry. Saving it links the card to the account. To add credits, choose Purchase Credits, review Quantity $, and confirm the amount before selecting Add Funds. The original article’s interface showed a USD 10 minimum; the platform’s current minimum takes precedence. Current Balance shows the available credits after processing. If you received a promotional credit code, use Redeem Code and follow the applicable redemption conditions. Auto-recharge Edit Auto-Recharge Settings controls the balance threshold and amount added. Enabling it can trigger further charges without a separate purchase each time. The source interface disables auto-recharge by setting Add $ to zero and saving. Confirm the actual disabled state in the current interface. Do not rely solely on an old screenshot. Insufficient credits can lead to stopped or deleted resources depending on provider support and platform policy. Keep independent backups of important data. Monitor usage Billing separates Compute Costs and Storage Costs. Review both. Detailed records can show totals by user or By Instance, which helps identify which environment is generating charges. 3. Choose a Launchable Open Launchables to browse deployable environments created by NVIDIA or the community. A Launchable bundles hardware requirements, software setup, and code for a particular application. The source uses an Isaac environment for Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab. See CAVEDU’s cloud Isaac Sim example for context. The details page shows hardware and an estimated price. Use Edit to inspect configuration and provider prices. The source recommends starting from the Launchable’s proposed specifications to reduce compatibility problems. Actual availability and billing can differ from estimates. Stop/start support matters Some provider environments support Stop/Start. Stopping ends compute usage for that environment, but retained storage may still be billed. Restarting depends on GPU availability; a stopped machine does not reserve future capacity. Environments without Stop/Start may need to be deleted when finished. Deletion removes that environment and its data, so export or back up anything important first. 4. Deploy and connect After reviewing the configuration and cost, Deploy Launchable provisions resources and runs its setup steps. Deployment time varies with available GPUs, hardware, and installation work. Connection options depend on the Launchable. The illustrated Isaac environment provides browser-based VS Code for files and commands, plus browser streaming for the Isaac Sim interface. 5. Finish by checking resources and costs Open GPUs to see environments that are running, stopped, or being deleted, together with their displayed hourly costs. Open each control panel as needed. Do not simply close the browser and assume billing has stopped. Verify resource state, check retained storage, and review auto-recharge settings. If deleting an environment, first confirm that its data is backed up and no longer needed. Official documentation The Docs navigation opens the official documentation. UI details, provider behavior, and pricing evolve, so use the current platform information for your actual account and deployment. English adaptation of CAVEDU’s original article. This link opens the CAVEDU website. Screenshots show the original walkthrough; payment details, rates, and policies must be checked on Brev at the time of use. No account creation, purchases, or cloud deployments were performed to prepare this article.

articles.title: Calling a model is a function call
articles.description: The client in my series is one fetch to the Messages API, no SDK, in a file called claude.ts, the only place the repository talks to the model. Its first question, what HTTP status 304 means, came back correct in 79 output tokens for $0.0008. Its second, how many days a customer has to return a lantern from a fictional company, came back as 323 tokens of advice and no answer, for $0.0033. Both were function calls: a string in, a string out, and a count of what it cost. Free, step by step: the video series at https://www.youtube.com/@JoelStevick and the site, https://joelstevick.com, with the demo and the book. Watch the episode: Calling a model from code Watch the episode: Prompts are code The request export async function ask(messages: Message[], options: Options = {}): Promise<Answer> { return { text: data.content.filter((b) => b.type === "text").map((b) => b.text).join(""), stopReason: data.stop_reason, inputTokens: data.usage.input_tokens, outputTokens: data.usage.output_tokens, cost: cost(data.usage), }; } Five fields. model is a constant at the top of the file, claude-sonnet-5-5; changing models is changing one line. max_tokens is the longest the answer may be, in tokens, 1,024 by default. system is the system prompt: instructions that sit above the conversation and apply to every turn of it. messages is the conversation, each message with a role, user or assistant. The model keeps no state between calls, so this list is everything it knows about the conversation. And effort is low: the model can reason before it answers, that hidden reasoning is billed as output tokens, and for lookups it is kept short. post is a fetch: method POST, a JSON body, and three headers, the content type, anthropic-version, which pins the API's behaviour to a dated version, and x-api-key, read from an environment variable. A response that is not OK throws with the status and the body. The response The response's content is a list of blocks, not a string; the client keeps the text blocks and joins them. stop_reason says why the answer ended: end_turn means the model finished, max_tokens means it hit the limit and was cut off. If your code parses what comes back, a cut-off answer is broken input, and stop_reason is how your code finds out. usage holds the token counts, input and output, as the server counted them, and the client turns them into dollars. Tokens and cost A token is a piece of text the model reads and writes as one unit, usually a few characters long. tokens.ts counts them through the count_tokens endpoint, which does not run the model and is free. One sentence from the series' documents, "The Firefly 220R charges in 3.5 hours over USB-C.", is 49 characters, 9 words, and 32 tokens. A short common word is one token; numbers, product names and punctuation split into several each. You cannot price a prompt by its word count. Count it. The price list is one constant: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. cost multiplies each count by its price and divides by a million. Output is five times the price of input, so a short question with a long answer is mostly paying for the answer: the 304 question was 27 tokens in and 79 out, about a twelfth of a cent, nearly all of it the answer. The context window is the most a model can take in one call, counted in tokens, prompt and answer together. Every request carries the whole conversation, so the input grows with every turn and you pay for the earlier turns again. The system prompt is sent on every call too. A question it cannot answer The company in my series is fictional. Its returns policy says 40 days from the delivery date. Asked for it, the model said it had no information about the company's policy and sent the customer to their receipt. That is the honest answer: nothing in the request put that file in front of it. It said so this time. A model that guessed a number instead would sound exactly as sure, and nothing in the response would tell you the number was guessed. The reply was 36 tokens in and 323 out, $0.0033 of advice. The fix is to put the right passage of that file in the request with the question. Prompts are code The next episode makes the output usable by code, two ways. Structured output is JSON in a shape you wrote. The shape is written twice: as a TypeScript type for the compiler, and as JSON Schema, a standard way to describe a JSON document's fields, their types and which are required, for the API, which constrains the answer to it. The code still parses the text with JSON.parse into unknown and checks it with a type guard, a function that returns true only when a value has the right shape, because the model's output is input to your program. And if the answer reaches max_tokens, the JSON is cut off and JSON.parse throws. The run turned a customer's email into an order id, a name, two items with quantities and the intent, return, for $0.0019. Tool use is the model asking your code to run a function. A tool is three things: a name, a description, and an input schema. const tools: Tool[] = [ { name: "lookup_order", description: "Look up one order by its id, such as LS-2026-004871. Returns the order as JSON.", input_schema: { type: "object", properties: { order_id: { type: "string", description: "The order id" } }, required: ["order_id"], }, ]; The model never runs the function. It answers with a tool_use block, a request with an id and the input; your code runs the function, appends the model's whole turn and a tool_result to the conversation, and calls again, in a while loop you wrote, until the model answers in text. The run took two round trips and cost $0.0046, and every fact in its answer came from data/orders.json. Look at what that added: a system prompt, a schema, and a tool description. They are strings and objects in TypeScript files, and they decide what the program does as much as any function does. Reword the description and you change when the model calls the tool. So they are treated as code: in the repository, reviewed in a pull request, and tested, from episode 7 on. The description is also in the request body on every call, so you pay for it as input every time. What to try next: at tag s1e2, run src/tokens.ts on a sentence from your own documents and compare its word count to its token count. Then at s1e3, add a second tool beside lookup_order with a one-sentence description, ask a question that could use either, and see which the model picks. First published at joelstevick.com/blog/calling-a-model-is-a-function-call. Watch the series: https://www.youtube.com/@JoelStevick. Everything else, the demo and the book included: https://joelstevick.com

I put my notes inside a physics simulation
articles.description: Most note apps show you a graph of your notes as a nice extra. I wanted the graph to be the app, and I wanted it to tell me something: which notes I actually use, and which ones I've forgotten. So I built Graph Notes: a note-taking app where every note is a body in a physics simulation. It has zero dependencies and is plain JavaScript. Try it in your browser: https://sathvik8317.github.io/graph-notes/ (it opens with demo notes) Repo: https://github.com/sathvik8317/graph-notes What it does Recency gravity. Notes you open or edit get pulled to the centre. Notes you haven't touched drift out to the edge. Colour goes from warm (recent) to cool (stale). After a few weeks of use the layout becomes a picture of what you're actually thinking about. Drag to link. Drop one note onto another in the graph and a Related: [[Target]] line gets added to the note you dragged. No typing. Time travel. Press Replay and watch the graph grow from your first note. Notes appear on the day you created them, and links appear when you first wrote them. It also has what you'd expect: Markdown with [[wikilinks]] (headings and aliases too), [[ autocomplete, backlinks, renames that rewrite every link, search, JSON export/import, dark mode and a phone layout. How the physics works I studied how Obsidian's graph view is put together (physics in a Web Worker, flat typed arrays, Barnes-Hut) and wrote my own engine in the style of d3-force. No Obsidian code is used. Each tick does four things: Link springs pull linked notes together. Many-body repulsion pushes every note away from every other note. Doing that pair by pair is O(n²), so it uses a Barnes-Hut quadtree (θ = 0.9): a far-away group of notes is treated as one heavy point. Gravity pulls each note towards the centre. Collision on a grid stops circles from overlapping. The engine runs in a Web Worker, so typing in the editor never stutters. Positions come back to the main thread as a transferred Float32Array, which is a handover rather than a copy. With 2,000 nodes a tick takes about 9 ms. Recency gravity turned out to be one line. Each note gets its own gravity multiplier: g = 0.25 + 2.75 * 0.5 ** (age / halfLife) A note you just touched gets 3x pull, and one you've ignored for a long time gets 0.25x. Repulsion does the rest and pushes the low-gravity notes outward. You set the half-life in the settings. Three bugs that taught me something The target ran away. My first drag-to-link never worked. Every note repels every other note, so when I dragged a note towards its target, the target slid away from it. The fix: while you hold a note, it becomes a "ghost" that doesn't repel or collide with anything. Links inside code blocks. If a note contains a code sample with [[something]] in it, that's not a link. The parser has to skip code spans and fenced blocks, or you get phantom edges. The camera. If you fit the view once on load, it fits the starting jumble and the graph then grows off screen. If you fit only once it settles, the screen is empty for a second. So it fits twice: once early so something is visible, and again when the layout settles, unless you've already panned or zoomed yourself. Try it The quickest way is the live demo: https://sathvik8317.github.io/graph-notes/ To run it locally, you need Node 20+ and nothing else: git clone https://github.com/sathvik8317/graph-notes cd graph-notes node serve.mjs # http://localhost:5173 It opens with demo notes so you can play with the graph right away. Notes are stored in your browser's localStorage, so use Export for backups. There are 21 tests covering the physics engine, the data model and the Markdown renderer (node --test test/). What's next Ghost links: on-device embeddings that suggest links between related notes you never connected Continents: detect clusters and give them names and soft outlines WebAssembly engine for very large graphs If you use a graph view in your own notes app: do you actually look at it, or is it just pretty? I'm curious whether recency gravity would change that for you.

articles.title: Browsers don't know how big your screen is: building an on-screen ring sizer
articles.description: I built Check My Ring Size, a free tool where you hold a ring up to your screen and match it to a circle. It sounds like a weekend project. The hard part is one sentence: a web page has no way to ask how big a millimeter is. If a circle is drawn 104 pixels wide, nothing in the browser tells you whether that is 17 mm on someone's phone or 30 mm on an old monitor. A ring that is 17.3 mm across (a US size 7) has to be drawn at exactly the right size, or the whole tool is worthless. This post is about how I solved that, and the bug that made my first version wrong by a factor of two to three. Why CSS units don't help CSS has mm and in, so it is tempting to write width: 17.3mm and move on. Don't. By definition, a CSS inch is 96 CSS pixels, and that is a reference value, not a measurement of your actual screen. On a real display, 17.3mm renders at whatever size the OS and panel happen to produce. It is only correct by accident. So the real problem is to find CSS pixels per millimeter (I call it pxPerMM) for this specific screen. Everything else is just drawing a circle at diameterMM * pxPerMM. I ended up supporting three ways to get that number, because every one of them fails for some people. Method 1: fingerprint the device The browser does tell you a few things: screen.width, screen.height and devicePixelRatio. Together they are a rough fingerprint. An iPhone 13 reports 390 x 844 CSS pixels at a ratio of 3. I keep a table of devices with those values and their published pixels per inch: ts export Two details matter. Portrait and landscape both have to match (rotated), and the ratio needs a tolerance, because browsers report values like 2.625 or 2.75 that don't equal the number on the spec sheet exactly. The bug The matched device gives me a published PPI, for example 460 for most recent iPhones. My first version did this: pxPerMM = match.ppi / 25.4; // wrong That gives 18.1 px per mm. It looks reasonable and it is badly wrong. Published PPI describes physical pixels. A CSS pixel on that iPhone is 3 physical pixels wide. The correct calculation divides by the device pixel ratio first: pxPerMM = match.ppi / dpr / 25.4; // 460 / 3 / 25.4 = about 6.04 At 18.1 px/mm, a 17.3 mm ring was drawn about 313 CSS pixels wide. At 6.04 px/mm it is about 104. Every circle on a high-density screen was exactly dpr times too large, so everyone would have been told to buy a ring that was far too small. It is the kind of bug that survives review, because every number looks plausible. I left a comment in the code explaining why the division exists, since it looks unnecessary until you know. The fingerprint approach has a weakness: it is a table I maintain, and different panels can share the same CSS size and ratio. That is why it is not the only method. Method 2: screen diagonal Most people know their screen size in inches ("a 24 inch monitor", "a 6.1 inch phone"). That is enough to calculate density without any device table. With the diagonal and the CSS resolution, the physical width follows from the aspect ratio: For a 1920 x 1080 monitor at 24 inches that works out to about 92 CSS pixels per inch. The method assumes square pixels and that the page isn't zoomed, so the UI tells people to reset browser zoom to 100 percent first. I also added a device search that fills the diagonal in automatically, because many people don't know it offhand. Method 3: hold a card or a coin to the screen The last method needs no database and no assumptions about the display. The user places a real object on the screen, a bank card (ISO ID-1, 85.6 x 53.98 mm) or a coin, and drags a slider until the on-screen shape matches its edges. Then: pxPerMM = sliderPx / objectWidthMM; This is the most trustworthy method, and the clunkiest, which is why it is the fallback. It also had its own bug. My slider originally ran from 80 to 500 pixels. A bank card fits that range on most screens, but a coin (around 23 mm) on a low-density screen needs only about 35 to 90 pixels, so the right answer was literally off the end of the slider. The fix is to scale the slider to the object, assuming screens fall somewhere between roughly 1.5 and 8 pixels per mm: // roughly 96 DPI After calibration Once pxPerMM is known, the rest is simple. The ring-size slider's pixel range is rebuilt from it so it always covers about 8 to 28 mm. The measured diameter is px / pxPerMM, and a lookup table maps that diameter to US, UK, EU, India, Japan and China sizes. Wide bands get a size bump, since a wide band fits tighter than a thin one at the same diameter. Lessons Never trust a number you can't connect to a physical object. Published PPI, CSS inches and the screen diagonal all looked plausible while being wrong or fragile. The only ground truth is something with a known real-world size. Test against a physical object. A unit test can happily confirm a wrong formula. Holding a real ring or card up to the screen is the check that catches it. Offer more than one route to the same value. Each method fails for somebody: unknown devices, unknown diagonals, no card to hand. Three paths to pxPerMM cover far more people than one clever path. Be honest about accuracy. An on-screen tool is good, not perfect. The guides on the site recommend measuring on two different days and comparing the result with a ring you already own that fits. The rest of the stack The site is Astro, static, on Cloudflare Pages, with six languages. Mobile Lighthouse performance went from 63 to 99, helped by not letting third-party scripts compete with first paint: ads and analytics load on the first user interaction (or after ten seconds as a fallback), and only the two most-used font files are preloaded. If you want to try the calibration yourself, the tool is free at checkmyringsize.com. I'd especially like to hear if auto-detect picks the wrong device on yours, since that is the part that depends on my device table.

articles.title: GeoServer probing: distinguishing exposure from confirmed compromise
articles.description: WatchTowr observed probing of two GeoServer vulnerabilities that appeared aimed at finding vulnerable servers. However, it had not reported successful remote code execution by attackers. Organizations operating GeoServer need to distinguish Internet exposure, vulnerable software and evidence of compromise when assessing their systems. Eye Security identified Internet-accessible servers, but that finding does not establish how many are vulnerable or compromised. TMGS emphasizes that asset inventory, vulnerability remediation and incident investigation each require their own evidence. Technical findings According to SecurityWeek, the two vulnerabilities being probed belong to a chain of five flaws discovered by Rapid7 researcher Jonah Burgess. Combined with other flaws, they can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. This does not establish that either vulnerability independently allows an attacker to take over a server. GeoServer has released patches. TMGS recommends upgrading to 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7. The absence of reported successful code execution is not a reason to delay remediation while probing is already being observed. TMGS recommendations TMGS recommends inventorying GeoServer deployments, recording their actual versions and Internet accessibility, and assigning someone to verify each upgrade. Prioritize Internet-accessible systems and restrict access according to business needs while updates are pending. For outsourced deployments, TMGS recommends obtaining the post-update version and functional test results from the responsible provider. Completion should include a confirmed version and a working service after the update. TMGS also recommends reviewing logs and unusual activity, documenting the limits of available evidence and assessing suspicious findings separately. Patching addresses vulnerabilities; conclusions about compromise require investigation evidence. Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/geoserver-va-khoang-cach-tu-do-quet-den-xam-nhap-i.2fd1ab87-f3af-46c4-a590-00e6d01a6f6e

articles.title: Context Propagation Across Goroutine Boundaries: Deadline Inheritance, Cancellation Races, and the Silent Leak
articles.description: The Problem With Implicit Deadline Inheritance Every production Go service eventually accumulates a category of goroutine leak that evades standard leak detectors: goroutines that are neither blocked nor idle, but consuming real resources while executing work whose results will never be observed. The usual culprit is not a missing defer cancel(). It is a structural mismatch between how context. Context deadlines propagate across goroutine boundaries and how the calling code reasons about cancellation. This article covers the mechanics of that mismatch, the race conditions it generates, and a propagation ownership model that prevents the failure mode at the design level. Deadline Propagation Is Not Goroutine Propagation When you derive a child context with context. WithDeadline or context. WithTimeout, the Go runtime registers a cancellation relationship. If the parent is cancelled, the child is cancelled. If the deadline elapses, the child's Done channel is closed. The child context carries the deadline value and the cancellation signal. What it does not carry is goroutine identity. The runtime has no notion of which goroutine "owns" a context. When you launch a goroutine and pass it a context derived from the request context, you are handing it a value, not a resource-lifetime contract. The goroutine is entirely responsible for observing the channel. func handleRequest(ctx context. Context, req *Request) error { childCtx, cancel := context. WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time. Second) defer cancel() go func() { result, err := callDownstream(childCtx, req) if err != nil { return } storeResult(result) // May execute after the HTTP response was sent. }() return nil The timeout fires after two seconds, closing childCtx. Done(). But callDownstream may already be inside a net. Dial that selects on a different internal channel. Whether the cancellation propagates correctly depends on whether callDownstream is built to observe ctx. Done() at every blocking point. If it is not, the goroutine runs to completion regardless. The calling function has exited. The HTTP handler has responded. The request span has ended. But the goroutine is live, holding a database connection, a Redis pipeline buffer, or an in-flight AWS SDK call. Three Distinct Failure Modes 1. Stale Context Completion The downstream completes successfully after the deadline. The result is written to a channel or shared structure. The consumer has already moved on. In a worker pool, this produces phantom completions that fill result channels which are no longer drained, causing goroutines waiting to send to block indefinitely. results := make(chan Result, 1) // Buffered by 1 — not by worker count. r, _ := callDownstream(ctx, req) results <- r // Blocks if the receiver already returned on ctx cancellation. select { case r := <-results: return r, nil case <-ctx. Done(): return nil, ctx. Err() The fix is not to increase buffer size. It is to make the goroutine itself select on ctx. Done() when sending. 2. Cancellation Race on Shared State When a parent context is cancelled and multiple goroutines share derived contexts from the same parent, all children receive the cancellation signal simultaneously. If those goroutines share a write target — a cache population path, an aggregation buffer, a distributed lock — you get concurrent writes from multiple cancelling goroutines. The classic manifestation in Redis pipelines: several goroutines detect cancellation, each attempts a cleanup write (e.g., decrement a counter, release a semaphore key), and the decrement executes multiple times because the check-and-act was not atomic. 3. Context Reuse Across Request Lifetimes Background goroutines launched with a request-scoped context that migrate to doing work beyond the request's logical scope. The pattern emerges in AI pipeline backends where a retrieval goroutine populates an embedding cache as a side effect of a user query. The request context carries the user's deadline. If the cache population is considered durable background work, it must run under a context derived from the service's root context, not the request context. Using context. Background() as the cache write context is correct here. Using the request context is a category error that causes cache writes to be abandoned when the client disconnects. Ownership Contracts: A Propagation Model The central discipline is treating context ownership as an explicit contract at every goroutine boundary. Three rules cover most production cases. Rule 1 — The launcher owns the cancel function. Whoever calls context. WithTimeout or context. WithCancel must call the returned cancel function, unconditionally, via defer. This is well-known. The subtler corollary: if the goroutine is expected to outlive the launcher's scope, the launcher must not pass a derived context — it must pass the parent context directly, or a new context derived from a scope that covers the goroutine's intended lifetime. Rule 2 — Goroutines that cannot observe cancellation must not receive cancellable contexts. If a goroutine performs blocking I/O that ignores the context (legacy libraries, raw syscalls, some CGO paths), passing a context to it is misleading. Wrap the call in a goroutine that the caller terminates by other means, or accept that the goroutine's lifetime is uncontrolled and account for that in pool sizing. Rule 3 — Result delivery must be cancellation-aware. Any goroutine that sends its result to a channel must select on ctx. Done() simultaneously. The result channel must be sized to the number of potential concurrent senders or senders must be able to drop results cleanly. func boundedFetch(ctx context. Context, req *Request) (Result, error) { type outcome struct { result Result err error ch := make(chan outcome, 1) r, err := callDownstream(ctx, req) case ch <- outcome{r, err}: case out := <-ch: return out.result, out.err return Result{}, ctx. Err() The goroutine will not leak because it selects on ctx. Done() before sending. The launcher's ctx. Done() and the goroutine's ctx. Done() are the same channel — same context, same signal. Deadline Skew in Layered Services In a microservice graph, deadline propagation via gRPC metadata or HTTP headers introduces skew. The upstream service sets a 500ms deadline. Network transit consumes 30ms. The downstream service extracts the deadline from metadata and reconstructs a context. The reconstructed deadline is now 470ms from the downstream's local clock — but only if the clocks are synchronized. In practice, NTP skew across ECS tasks or EC2 instances within the same region is small (single-digit milliseconds), but across regions or when an instance has not synced recently, skew can reach tens of milliseconds. For services with tight latency budgets, this means the downstream may believe it has more time than the upstream expects. The conservative approach: propagate the absolute deadline timestamp in metadata, reconstruct with a small safety margin subtracted, and log the computed remaining budget. This makes deadline skew observable rather than invisible. func extractDeadlineContext(ctx context. Context, md metadata.MD) (context. Context, context. CancelFunc) { vals := md. Get("x-deadline-unix-ms") if len(vals) == 0 { return context. WithCancel(ctx) ms, err := strconv. ParseInt(vals[0], 10, 64) deadline := time. UnixMilli(ms).Add(-10 * time. Millisecond) // Safety margin. return context. WithDeadline(ctx, deadline) Observability: Surfacing Context Violations Context leaks are silent by default. Three instrumentation points make them detectable. Goroutine count delta per request. Export runtime. NumGoroutine() as a gauge before and after request handling. Persistent upward drift correlated with request rate is a leak signal. This is coarse but catches systemic problems. Span annotations for deadline budget. At each service boundary, record the remaining deadline budget as a span attribute: deadline_remaining_ms. When a trace shows a downstream span starting with a negative or near-zero budget, the upstream is sending already-expired contexts — a logic error, not a network problem. Cancel cause logging. Go 1.21 introduced context. WithCancelCause and context. Cause. Wrapping cancellations with a cause allows middleware to log why a context was cancelled rather than just that it was. In a request pipeline that fans out to MongoDB, Redis, and an external AI inference endpoint, knowing which leg triggered the cascade is essential for distinguishing timeouts from client disconnects from upstream failures. Decision Framework When reviewing a goroutine launch or a context handoff in production code, apply these checks in order: Lifetime alignment. Does the goroutine's intended lifetime match the context's deadline? If not, derive from a longer-lived context or use context. Background() explicitly and document why. Cancellation observability. Does every blocking call inside the goroutine accept a context and propagate cancellation? If not, the context is decorative — remove the false safety it implies and handle the goroutine's lifecycle by other means. Result channel safety. Does the goroutine select on ctx. Done() when delivering results? A goroutine that can block on a channel send is a goroutine that can leak. Clock and skew budget. For cross-service deadline propagation, is the deadline transmitted as an absolute timestamp? Is a margin applied on reconstruction? Is the remaining budget observable in traces? Cancellation side effects. Does cancellation of the context trigger any writes or cleanup operations? If multiple goroutines share the same cancellation signal, are those operations idempotent and safe for concurrent execution? Context propagation is not a convenience API. It is a distributed coordination primitive. Treating goroutine boundaries as invisible to that primitive is the root cause of most production context-related leaks, races, and observability gaps in Go services.

articles.title: I built a Telegram alert relay that never sees portfolio data
articles.description: I built a Telegram alert relay that never sees portfolio data FolioSpan is a local-first portfolio tracker. When users asked for Telegram delivery of price alerts, the obvious design — send the portfolio to a server, evaluate there, forward the alert — was off the table. The app's whole point is that holdings never leave the device unless you opt in. So the relay is deliberately blind. The shape of it Alert evaluation happens on-device. The app periodically checks prices in the background and composes the finished notification text locally — "Portfolio value crossed 1.00", "BTC moved -6.2% in 24h". The worker is a dumb pipe. A Cloudflare Worker exposes /link, /webhook, /send, /status. Its KV stores only an opaque link token mapped to a chat ID. No holdings, no prices, no portfolio — ever. Linking is one-shot. The app opens a t.me/bot?start= URL; the token is single-use with a 10-minute TTL. /stop in Telegram wipes the binding from KV, and the app clears its local credentials on the next status check. The message travels verbatim. The client posts the finished text to /send; the worker relays it to Telegram HTML-escaped, capped at 3,500 chars and 60 messages/day. What that buys If the relay is compromised tomorrow, the attacker gets a table of random tokens and chat IDs — not a single holding. The privacy contract isn't "we promise not to look"; it's that there is nothing to look at. Trade-offs I accepted No two-way bot. /stop is the only command; anything else gets a help message. Query commands like /portfolio would require the server to see holdings — a different product, not a toggle. Local-time semantics. Quiet hours and the daily fire cap are enforced by the on-device policy engine before a message is ever produced — the relay doesn't need to know about them. The full feature note is on the blog: https://getfoliospan.com/blog/price-alerts-without-brokerage App: https://getfoliospan.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=free2026

articles.title: How the FAA's new Line Up and Wait rules may impact Thanksgiving holiday air travel
articles.description: The Federal Aviation Administration imposed new standards for its Line Up and Wait airport policy on Tuesday that, though not a significant change, could affect travelers during the busy holiday travel season. Line Up and Wait (LUAW) is a procedure that allows planes preparing for departure from busy airports to taxi into position on the runway while they wait to be cleared for takeoff. It’s designed to make airport departures more efficient by putting planes in position to take off as soon as airspace has been cleared. Under the FAA’s new policy, airports can still use LUAW, but they must designate a watch supervisor whose sole job is to oversee LUAW operations and whose attention cannot be split by other tasks. The new rules change guidance from saying that airports “should” have a dedicated LUAW supervisor to saying that they “must” have one. The FAA said the change is intended to “elevate the safety standard” for LUAW operations by “removing ambiguity” about staffing requirements under the old rules. Will the new rules affect Thanksgiving holiday travel? The impact of the policy change on passengers comes down to staffing. At airports with enough staff to assign one person exclusively to LUAW, the effect will likely be minimal. But airports that may be short-staffed, a chronic problem in recent years, might be unable to use LUAW. That could mean slightly longer waits on the tarmac in some cases. Even minor delays caused by the new LUAW policy could be compounded by potential disruptions from the Thanksgiving travel rush, with 417,000 flights expected to depart during the 9-day holiday travel period and stormy weather forecast for both coasts. The new LUAW rules will also be in place for the December holiday travel season. They are scheduled to expire in June. FAA under scrutiny Though the new policy represents a relatively minor procedural update, it comes at a time when the FAA is under intense scrutiny following the historically disruptive nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of 18,000 flights earlier this month. That outage, plus a series of smaller technical disruptions in the weeks since, has fueled a sense of “outage anxiety” among holiday travelers. In a recent YouGov poll, 72% of respondents said they were concerned about "flight cancellations or significant delays as a result of further disruptions to U.S. air travel" over the holiday travel season. Nearly a third said the ground stop could potentially lead them to alter their travel plans. The new LUAW rules are not related to the ground stop or other recent disruptions. They were first proposed in early October, more than a month before the ground stop occurred. There were no reports of significant delays related to the new rules on Tuesday, the first day they were in effect and the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel season. Congress is debating whether to provide the FAA with billions of dollars in additional funding to upgrade its infrastructure and implement other changes to prevent future outages. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has asked for $50 billion, but even lawmakers who support a funding boost for the FAA say the final price tag could be much smaller. The debate could affect LUAW operations at the nation’s airports, depending on whether Congress approves funding to help them address staffing shortages that may limit their ability to assign someone exclusively to LUAW. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Travel at https://travel.yahoo.com/news/article/new-faa-rule-line-up-and-wait-impact-on-thanksgiving-holiday-air-travel-174323076.html
